config.title: The Leaning Tower of Pisa: 835 years of not falling over

events.label:
Construction starts.
Soil: soft. Optimism: high.
events.note: Foundations laid on 9 August 1173, on soft clay and sand; work on the ground floor begins a few days later.

events.label:
Second floor reached.
The tower starts to lean.
events.note: The ground on the south side gives way. Wars with Genoa, Lucca and Florence soon stop the works for almost a century, which lets the soil consolidate and is probably the reason the tower is still standing.

events.label:
Works resume: upper floors
built taller on one side
events.note: Giovanni di Simone tries to correct the tilt by making the new floors taller on the low side. The result is a slightly curved tower: the banana is a design feature.

events.label:
Pisa loses at Meloria.
Pause, again.
events.note: Defeat by the Genoese at the Battle of Meloria halts construction once more.

events.label:
Bell chamber added:
done in only 199 years
events.note: Tommaso di Andrea Pisano completes the bell chamber. The bells were later silenced, for fear their vibrations could make things worse.

events.label:
Galileo (allegedly) drops
two balls from the top
events.note: The story comes from Vincenzo Viviani's biography of Galileo, written in 1654 and published in 1717. Historians doubt the experiment ever took place, at least not from here.

events.label:
A walkway is dug around
the base. Tilt: increases.
events.note: Alessandro Della Gherardesca excavates a walkway (the 'catino') to expose the buried base. Water floods in on the south side and the inclination increases noticeably.

events.label:
Foundation strengthened
with grout. Tilt: increases.
events.note: Engineers drill 361 holes in the foundation and inject 80 tonnes of grout; the tilt jumps by 31 arc seconds. Popular accounts credit Mussolini with ordering the tower straightened.

events.label:
Italy asks the world for help
(but please keep the tilt)
events.note: On 27 February 1964 the Italian government requests international help to prevent the collapse, while making clear the lean is to be preserved: it is good for tourism.

events.label:
Tilt reaches 5.5°.
Closed to the public.
events.note: The tower is closed on 7 January 1990.

events.label:
Lead counterweights, then
soil gently removed from
under the high side
events.note: 870 tonnes of lead are placed on the north side from 1993; later, about 70 tonnes of soil are extracted from beneath it. The top moves back by about 45 cm, to where it was in 1838.

events.label:
Reopened: "stable for
at least 300 years"
events.note: The tower reopens to visitors on 15 December 2001.

events.label:
It has stopped moving,
for the first time ever
events.note: In May 2008 engineers announce that the tower has stopped moving for the first time in its history. Current tilt: about 3.97°.
